summary: Jonah prays to Yahweh from inside the fish, describing his descent into the sea as a near-death crisis and his rescue as God’s answer. The prayer moves from distress and remembered abandonment to thanksgiving, vows, and the confession that salvation belongs to Yahweh. The chapter ends when Yahweh speaks to the fish and Jonah is put back on dry land.
whyItMatters: This chapter turns the sea rescue into a prayer of thanksgiving before Jonah receives his second commission. It shows Jonah grateful for mercy to himself, a theme the rest of the book will test when mercy is extended to Nineveh.

context.author: The book narrates events about Jonah son of Amittai but does not identify its author.
context.audience: No audience is named; the story addresses readers familiar with Israel’s God and presses questions about mercy, wrongdoing, and outsiders.
context.date: The narrated Jonah is linked with the eighth century BCE through 2 Kings, but the book’s composition date is disputed and no exact year is secure.
context.setting: This chapter takes place inside the fish after Jonah has been thrown into the sea and before he is returned to dry land.
context.literaryForm: A prophetic story with a poetic thanksgiving prayer embedded in the narrative.

outline.heading: Prayer from the fish
outline.note: Jonah prays to Yahweh, his God, from the fish’s belly.

outline.heading: Distress and answer
outline.note: He says he called from affliction and from the belly of Sheol, and that Yahweh heard him.

outline.heading: Descent into the sea
outline.note: Jonah describes being cast into the depths, surrounded by waters, and barred in, yet brought up from the pit by Yahweh.

outline.heading: Remembering Yahweh
outline.note: As his soul faints, Jonah remembers Yahweh, and his prayer comes into God’s holy temple.

outline.heading: Thanksgiving and vow
outline.note: Jonah contrasts vain idols with mercy and promises sacrifice, thanksgiving, and fulfilled vows, ending with salvation belonging to Yahweh.

outline.heading: Returned to dry land
outline.note: Yahweh speaks to the fish, and it vomits Jonah onto dry land.

keyVerses.text: Then Jonah prayed to Yahweh, his God, out of the fish’s belly.
keyVerses.why: This verse locates the whole prayer inside the fish and identifies it as speech to Yahweh, not simply reflection.

keyVerses.text: He said, “I called because of my affliction to Yahweh. He answered me. Out of the belly of Sheol I cried. You heard my voice.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the basic movement of the prayer: distress, crying out, and being heard.

keyVerses.text: I went down to the bottoms of the mountains. The earth barred me in forever; yet you have brought my life up from the pit, Yahweh my God.
keyVerses.why: This verse captures both the depth of Jonah’s danger and his claim that Yahweh rescued his life.

keyVerses.text: But I will sacrifice to you with the voice of thanksgiving. I will pay that which I have vowed. Salvation belongs to Yahweh.”
keyVerses.why: This verse brings the prayer to its theological climax: Jonah promises thanksgiving and names salvation as Yahweh’s.

questions.question: Where is Jonah when he prays this chapter?
questions.answer: Jonah prays from the fish’s belly, and his release onto dry land comes after the prayer. WEB 2:1–10 corresponds to Hebrew, Douay-Rheims, and Brenton 2:2–11; those editions place the swallowing at 2:1, where WEB has 1:17.

questions.question: Is Jonah confessing his refusal to go to Nineveh here?
questions.answer: The prayer thanks Yahweh for hearing and rescuing him, and it promises sacrifice and vows. It does not explicitly confess Jonah’s earlier flight from his commission. His later anger in chapter 4 also cautions against treating this prayer as a complete change in every part of his attitude.

questions.question: What does “Sheol” mean in this prayer?
questions.answer: Sheol is the realm of the dead. Jonah describes crying from its belly, then being brought up from the pit. The prayer uses this death imagery to express overwhelming danger and rescue; the narrative does not separately report Jonah dying and being raised.

questions.question: Why does Jonah say God threw him into the sea when the sailors did it?
questions.answer: Jonah says, “you threw me into the depths,” even though the previous chapter describes sailors throwing him into the sea. Within the prayer, Jonah interprets the event as under Yahweh’s rule. The chapter itself focuses on God’s agency in rescue as well as judgment.

questions.question: What is the “holy temple” doing in a prayer from the sea?
questions.answer: Jonah recalls feeling banished from God’s sight but expects to look toward the holy temple again. Later he says his prayer reached God there. The repeated temple image connects his distress at sea with hope of renewed access to God.

questions.question: Does the chapter identify what kind of fish swallowed Jonah?
questions.answer: WEB calls it a fish and gives no biological description. Brenton calls it a whale, including in its prayer introduction at 2:2, corresponding to WEB 2:1. The Hebrew phrase for the creature means a great fish, so a modern species cannot be established from these names alone.

questions.question: What are “vain idols” in verse 8?
questions.answer: The phrase names objects of trust or worship that cannot give what Yahweh gives. Jonah says those who regard them “forsake their own mercy.” The verse is a compact contrast between unreliable devotion and the mercy Jonah has just described receiving.

questions.question: Why does Jonah promise sacrifice and vows?
questions.answer: Jonah responds to rescue by promising sacrifice with thanksgiving and fulfillment of what he has vowed. These commitments echo the sailors’ sacrifice and vows in the preceding chapter. The story records his intention here without yet showing him carrying it out after reaching land.

questions.question: What does “Salvation belongs to Yahweh” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, it summarizes Jonah’s experience that his rescue did not come from himself. He was surrounded by waters and described as barred in, yet says Yahweh brought his life up from the pit. The final narrative action reinforces that claim when Yahweh commands the fish and Jonah reaches dry land.

glossary.def: Jonah’s distress or trouble; he says he called to Yahweh because of it.
The realm of the dead in the language of the prayer; here it is part of Jonah’s description of extreme danger and rescue.
The place Jonah looks toward and says his prayer reaches.
Promised; Jonah says he will fulfill what he has promised to Yahweh.
The place where the fish releases Jonah after Yahweh speaks to it.
